questions.stem: hCG shares an identical alpha subunit with which of the following hormones?
explanations: Oxytocin and vasopressin are small peptide hormones structurally unrelated to hCG.
Correct. hCG is a heterodimeric glycoprotein hormone with an alpha subunit identical to LH, FSH, and TSH; the beta subunit confers hormone specificity.
Insulin and glucagon are pancreatic peptide hormones unrelated to hCG's structure.
Prolactin, growth hormone, and cortisol are not glycoprotein hormones sharing hCG's alpha subunit structure.
questions.overview: hCG is a heterodimeric glycoprotein hormone composed of an alpha subunit identical to that of LH, FSH, and TSH, and a unique beta subunit that confers its specific biological activity. Its similarity to LH allows it to bind LH receptors on the corpus luteum, maintaining progesterone secretion in early pregnancy, and its similarity to TSH explains why very high hCG levels can cause hyperthyroidism.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man taking a diuretic for heart failure develops bilateral breast enlargement. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible, given its anti-androgen effect?
explanations: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that is not described as causing gynecomastia through anti-androgen effects.
Metoprolol is a beta-blocker and is not listed as a cause of gynecomastia.
Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic not associated with gynecomastia in the notes.
Correct. Spironolactone is a classic drug that causes gynecomastia through its anti-androgen effects.
questions.overview: Gynecomastia refers to breast development in males and can be physiologic (newborns, puberty, older age) or drug-induced. Classic anti-androgenic drugs causing gynecomastia include spironolactone (a diuretic), cimetidine (an H2 blocker), and ketoconazole (an antifungal), as well as conditions like cirrhosis and Klinefelter syndrome.

questions.stem: A testicular germ cell tumor composed of nests of large cells with clear cytoplasm and central nuclei, described as having a 'fried egg' appearance, is most consistent with:
explanations: Embryonal carcinoma shows a mass with hemorrhage/necrosis, distinct from the homogeneous 'fried egg' seminoma appearance.
Choriocarcinoma shows syncytiotrophoblast/cytotrophoblast cells without villi, not fried egg cells.
Correct. Seminoma is composed of undifferentiated germ cells with the classic 'fried egg' appearance, and grossly is a homogeneous grey-white mass without hemorrhage or necrosis.
Yolk sac tumor shows Schiller-Duval (glomeruloid) bodies, not fried egg cells.
questions.overview: Seminoma is the most common testicular germ cell tumor, presenting as a homogeneous grey-white mass without hemorrhage or necrosis, with characteristic 'fried egg' histology; it is the male counterpart of ovarian dysgerminoma. Seminomas remain localized longer than non-seminomatous germ cell tumors, spread first to lymph nodes, and are highly curable.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with sickle cell disease presents with a painful erection lasting 6 hours that is unrelated to sexual activity. Aspiration of cavernosal blood reveals hypoxia and acidosis. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this presentation?
options: Localized fibrosis of the tunica albuginea (Peyronie disease)
Failure of cavernosal venous outflow causing ischemic priapism
An arterial-cavernosal fistula from prior perineal trauma causing high-flow priapism
explanations: Dopamine excess is not a described mechanism of priapism in this context.
Peyronie disease causes penile curvature and nodularity from tunica albuginea fibrosis, not persistent painful erection.
PDE5 inhibitor use can cause priapism as a side effect, but this patient's priapism is attributed to his sickle cell disease, not medication use.

Correct. Ischemic priapism accounts for 95% of cases and results from failure of cavernosal venous outflow (veno-occlusion), classically caused by sickle cell disease, leading to hypoxia and acidosis of trapped penile blood.
Arteriovenous fistula from trauma causes non-ischemic, high-flow priapism, which is not typically associated with sickle cell disease or with hypoxic, acidotic cavernosal blood.
questions.overview: Priapism is a persistent erection lasting more than 2-4 hours unrelated to sexual stimulation; 95% of cases are ischemic (low-flow), resulting from failure of cavernosal venous outflow, classically due to sickle cell veno-occlusion or vasoactive drugs (antipsychotics, alpha blockers, PDE5 inhibitors). This causes hypoxia and acidosis of penile blood and is a urologic emergency treated with corporal aspiration, intracavernosal phenylephrine, or surgery to prevent permanent erectile dysfunction and necrosis.

questions.stem: The blood-testis barrier formed by tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells serves primarily to:
options: Allow FSH to directly stimulate spermatogonia
Enable Leydig cells to secrete testosterone into the tubule lumen
Isolate developing sperm antigens from the immune system
Prevent oxytocin from reaching myoepithelial cells
explanations: The barrier does not facilitate FSH action; spermatogonia remain on the basal side outside the barrier.
Leydig cells are in the interstitium outside the seminiferous tubules and secrete testosterone there, not through the blood-testis barrier into the lumen.
Correct. The blood-testis barrier isolates developing sperm (post-meiotic antigens) to protect them from autoimmune attack.
Oxytocin acts on myoepithelial cells in the breast, unrelated to the testicular blood-testis barrier.
questions.overview: Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubules, support developing spermatozoa, and form the blood-testis barrier via tight junctions, separating the basal compartment (spermatogonia) from the apical compartment (meiosis and spermiogenesis). This barrier isolates the antigenically distinct, post-meiotic germ cells from the immune system, and Sertoli cell function is stimulated by FSH and supported by paracrine testosterone from Leydig cells.

questions.stem: Finasteride is used in the treatment of BPH because it inhibits which enzyme?
explanations: 11-beta hydroxylase is an adrenal steroidogenesis enzyme unrelated to BPH treatment.
Flutamide, not finasteride, is a competitive androgen receptor antagonist used in prostate cancer.
Correct. Finasteride is a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, blocking conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), the hormone driving BPH growth.
Aromatase converts androgens to estrogens and is not the target of finasteride.
questions.overview: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is an age-related hyperplasia of stromal and epithelial prostate cells driven by dihydrotestosterone (DHT); finasteride, a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, blocks conversion of testosterone to DHT and provides slow-onset symptom relief, while alpha-1 blockers and PDE-5 inhibitors relieve symptoms via smooth muscle relaxation.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of an erythematous, scaly, eczematous change of the nipple and areola that has not improved with topical corticosteroids. She also reports intermittent bloody nipple discharge. Biopsy of the nipple epidermis reveals large cells with clear halos infiltrating singly through the epidermis. Which of the following best explains this presentation?
options: Ductal carcinoma in situ extending to the nipple epidermis
explanations: LCIS does not extend to the nipple skin and does not produce Paget cells or nipple eczema.
Contact dermatitis would be expected to improve with topical steroids and would not show malignant epidermal cells on biopsy.
Intraductal papilloma classically causes bloody/serous discharge with a small subareolar mass, but not an eczematous nipple lesion with malignant epidermal cells.
Fibrocystic changes are benign and do not produce malignant Paget cells in the nipple epidermis.

Correct. Paget disease of the breast occurs when underlying DCIS extends along the ducts into the nipple epidermis, producing malignant Paget cells and an eczematous, erythematous nipple lesion, often with bloody discharge.
questions.overview: Paget disease of the breast is caused by underlying ductal carcinoma in situ (or invasive carcinoma) extending along the lactiferous ducts into the nipple epidermis, producing malignant Paget cells and a clinically eczematous, erythematous nipple lesion often with bloody discharge. More than half of patients have a palpable mass, and most cases ultimately reveal invasive carcinoma, so it must be distinguished from benign nipple dermatitis.

questions.stem: The most important risk factor for placenta accreta is:
explanations: Advanced maternal age is not specifically listed as the key risk factor for accreta.
Correct. Prior cesarean section, especially combined with placenta previa, is the most important risk factor for placenta accreta due to defective uterine decidualization at the scar site.
Maternal smoking is listed as a risk factor for placental abruption, not accreta.
Multiple gestation is not identified as the most important risk factor for abnormal placental attachment.
questions.overview: Placenta accreta spectrum (accreta, increta, percreta) results from defective decidualization of the uterus, allowing the placenta to attach directly to or invade through the myometrium; the most important risk factor is prior cesarean section, particularly combined with placenta previa. Undetected abnormal attachment can cause the placenta to fail to detach after delivery, leading to massive postpartum hemorrhage often requiring hysterectomy.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old G1P0 woman at 34 weeks' gestation presents with new headache and right upper quadrant pain. Blood pressure is 156/98 mmHg. Laboratory studies show schistocytes on peripheral smear, elevated total bilirubin, low haptoglobin, AST/ALT elevation, and a platelet count of 65,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Placental abruption classically presents with painful vaginal bleeding and uterine tenderness/contractions, not this hemolytic and hepatic laboratory pattern.
Uncomplicated preeclampsia would not be expected to show hemolysis (schistocytes, low haptoglobin) or significant thrombocytopenia; this patient has the more severe HELLP variant.
Gestational hypertension does not include proteinuria, hemolysis, or organ dysfunction, which are present here.
Eclampsia requires the presence of seizures, which are not described in this vignette.

Correct. HELLP syndrome is a severe variant of preeclampsia defined by microangiopathic Hemolysis (schistocytes, elevated bilirubin, low haptoglobin), Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets, resulting from coagulation activation and hepatic infarction.
questions.overview: HELLP syndrome is a severe complication of preeclampsia characterized by microangiopathic Hemolysis (schistocytes, elevated bilirubin, low haptoglobin), Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets, reflecting coagulation activation and hepatic infarction; definitive treatment is delivery. It shares the same underlying pathophysiology as preeclampsia — abnormal trophoblastic invasion of spiral arteries leading to placental hypoperfusion and diffuse maternal endothelial dysfunction.

questions.stem: Division of a fertilized zygote within the first 3 days after fertilization most likely results in which placental/membrane configuration for monozygotic twins?
explanations: Monochorionic monoamniotic results from division on days 9-12, after both chorion and amnion are developing.
Conjoined twins result from division on day 13 or later, well past day 3.
Monochorionic diamniotic results from division on days 4-8, after chorion development has begun, not within days 1-3.
Correct. Division within days 1-3 after fertilization, before chorion development begins, results in dichorionic, diamniotic twins, similar to dizygotic twins.
questions.overview: The placental and membrane configuration of monozygotic twins depends on the timing of zygote division: division within days 1-3 yields dichorionic diamniotic twins, division on days 4-8 yields monochorionic diamniotic twins, division on days 9-12 yields monochorionic monoamniotic twins (higher risk), and division on day 13 or later results in conjoined twins.

questions.stem: Failure of fusion between which structures leads to cleft lip?
options: Maxillary prominences and medial nasal prominences
Lateral nasal prominences and mandibular prominences
explanations: Correct. Maxillary prominences (from the first pharyngeal arch) normally fuse with the medial nasal prominences to form the primary palate; failure of this fusion causes cleft lip.
This fusion event is not described in the notes as the cause of cleft lip.
Fusion of the palatine shelves forms the secondary palate; failure causes cleft palate, not cleft lip.
Fusion between lateral nasal prominences and mandibular prominences is not the process that forms the primary palate in the notes.
questions.overview: Cleft lip results from failure of the maxillary prominences (derived from the first pharyngeal arch) to fuse with the medial nasal prominences, which normally forms the primary palate and philtrum. This is distinct from cleft palate, which results from failure of fusion of the lateral palatine shelves forming the secondary palate.

questions.stem: DiGeorge syndrome results from failure of development of which pharyngeal pouches?
explanations: The 1st pouch forms the eustachian tube/middle ear and the 2nd forms the palatine tonsil lining; failure of these is not linked to DiGeorge syndrome.
Correct. DiGeorge syndrome results from failure of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches, causing absent thymus and parathyroid glands, most commonly from a 22q11 deletion.
The 2nd pouch is not implicated in DiGeorge syndrome.
DiGeorge syndrome is attributed specifically to 3rd/4th pouch failure, not all four pouches.
questions.overview: DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia) results from failure of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches to develop, most commonly due to a 22q11 chromosomal deletion, producing the classic triad of absent thymus, absent parathyroid glands (hypocalcemia/tetany), and conotruncal congenital heart defects. The third pouch normally forms the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands, while the fourth forms the superior parathyroid glands and the ultimobranchial body (thyroid C-cells).

questions.stem: Which ovarian tumor type is classically associated with psammoma bodies and is the most common malignant ovarian epithelial tumor?
explanations: Correct. Serous cystadenocarcinoma is the most common malignant ovarian tumor, with cells resembling fallopian tube epithelium and characteristic psammoma bodies.
Endometrioid tumors resemble endometrium and are associated with endometriosis, not psammoma bodies.
Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma secretes mucous and may lead to pseudomyxoma peritonei, but is not classically associated with psammoma bodies.
Brenner tumor contains transitional epithelial cells with 'coffee bean' nuclei and is usually benign, not linked to psammoma bodies.
questions.overview: Serous tumors are the most common ovarian epithelial tumor type, and serous cystadenocarcinoma is the most common malignant ovarian tumor overall; it forms complex cysts lined by cells resembling fallopian tube epithelium and characteristically contains psammoma bodies. This contrasts with mucinous tumors (larger, multiloculated, can cause pseudomyxoma peritonei) and endometrioid tumors (associated with endometriosis, generally better prognosis).

questions.stem: Which of the following best distinguishes a phyllodes tumor from a fibroadenoma of the breast?
options: Only fibroadenomas can undergo malignant transformation
Fibroadenomas arise from ductal epithelium while phyllodes tumors arise from lobular epithelium
Phyllodes tumors typically occur in women older than 60, while fibroadenomas occur in women 15-35 years old
Phyllodes tumors are hormone-sensitive while fibroadenomas are not
explanations: This is reversed: high-grade phyllodes tumor variants, not fibroadenomas, can metastasize.
Both fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor are stromal (fibroepithelial) tumors arising from intralobular stroma, not directly from epithelium.
Correct. Fibroadenoma occurs in premenopausal women (ages 15-35) and is hormone-sensitive, while phyllodes tumor typically presents in older women (>60 years).
This is reversed: fibroadenomas, not phyllodes tumors, are described as clearly hormone-sensitive, increasing in size with the menstrual cycle and pregnancy.
questions.overview: Fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor are both benign stromal (fibroepithelial) tumors of the breast arising from intralobular stroma, but they occur at different ages: fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast tumor of premenopausal women (15-35 years) and is hormone-sensitive, whereas phyllodes tumor typically presents in older women (>60) and, unlike fibroadenoma, has high-grade variants capable of metastasis.

questions.stem: On pelvic ultrasound, an ovarian cyst demonstrating a thick wall with peripheral 'ring of fire' vascularity is most consistent with:
explanations: Dermoid cysts have characteristic ultrasound features related to fat, hair, and calcification, not ring of fire vascularity.
Theca-lutein cysts are usually bilateral and multiple, associated with very high hCG, but are not specifically described with ring of fire vascularity.
Correct. Corpus luteal cysts are thick-walled with 'ring of fire' vascularity on ultrasound, in contrast to thin-walled, avascular follicular cysts.
Follicular cysts are described as thin-walled with no vascularity on ultrasound, not 'ring of fire.'
questions.overview: Functional ovarian cysts arise from normal ovarian structures — follicular cysts form when a follicle fails to rupture (thin-walled and avascular on ultrasound), while corpus luteal cysts form when the corpus luteum fails to involute (thick-walled with 'ring of fire' vascularity, may delay menstruation). Both can present with pelvic pain and an adnexal mass.

questions.stem: In limb bud development, removal of the apical ectodermal ridge (AER) followed by replacement with a bead soaked in which factor restores normal proximal-to-distal limb growth?
explanations: Correct. Replacing the removed AER with FGF restores normal proximal-to-distal limb growth, since FGF is the key signal maintaining the progress zone of proliferating mesoderm.
Wnt-7a governs the dorsal-ventral limb axis by dorsalizing the underlying mesoderm, not proximal-distal growth.
Retinoic acid is not described as the factor that restores AER function in the notes.
Sonic hedgehog is the key signal from the zone of polarizing activity governing the anterior-posterior axis, not the AER-associated proximal-distal signal.
questions.overview: The apical ectodermal ridge (AER) is essential for proximal-to-distal limb growth by maintaining a 'progress zone' of proliferating mesoderm beneath it, mediated by fibroblast growth factor (FGF); removing the AER halts limb growth, but replacing it with an FGF-soaked bead restores normal growth. This is distinct from Sonic hedgehog (anterior-posterior axis) and Wnt-7a (dorsal-ventral axis).

questions.stem: Potter sequence, in which decreased amniotic fluid leads to external compression of the fetus, abnormal facies, and pulmonary hypoplasia, is classified as which type of error in morphogenesis?
explanations: Disruption refers to normal tissue growth being arrested by an external force (e.g., amniotic band syndrome), which is different from altered shape without arrest.
Agenesis is an intrinsic error where an organ is missing due to absent embryonic tissue (e.g., renal agenesis), not an extrinsic mechanical process.
Correct. Deformation is an extrinsic error where an external force leads to abnormal growth or shape (not arrest) of a structure, and Potter sequence is the classic example.
Malformation is an intrinsic abnormality in structure development (e.g., neural tube defects, cleft lip/palate), not an external force altering an otherwise normally forming structure.
questions.overview: Errors in morphogenesis are divided into intrinsic causes (agenesis, aplasia, hypoplasia, malformation) and extrinsic causes (disruption and deformation). Potter sequence is the classic example of deformation: absent/decreased amniotic fluid (usually from fetal renal failure) removes fetal cushioning, leading to external compression causing abnormal facies, limb positioning, and pulmonary hypoplasia.

questions.stem: The HPV E7 oncoprotein contributes to cervical carcinogenesis primarily by:
options: Inhibiting the p53 tumor suppressor protein
Inducing integration of viral DNA into the host mitochondrial genome
Inhibiting the Rb tumor suppressor protein, releasing E2F
explanations: Telomerase activation is not a described mechanism for E7.
Inhibiting p53 is the function of the HPV E6 protein, not E7.
Mitochondrial DNA integration is not a mechanism discussed for HPV oncogenesis.

Correct. The E7 gene product inhibits the Rb tumor suppressor protein; since Rb normally sequesters the E2F transcription factor, its inhibition releases E2F to drive uncontrolled cell cycle progression.
questions.overview: High-risk HPV subtypes (16 and 18) drive cervical, anal, penile, and oropharyngeal cancers through two key oncogenes: E6, which inhibits the p53 tumor suppressor, and E7, which inhibits the Rb tumor suppressor, together producing uncontrolled cell cycle progression. Persistent HPV infection drives progression through cervical intraepithelial neoplasia to invasive carcinoma, detectable at the precursor stage by Pap smear (koilocytes).

questions.stem: A newborn with a 46,XX karyotype is found to have ambiguous genitalia with clitoromegaly and fused labioscrotal folds. On day 5 of life, the infant develops vomiting, lethargy, hyperkalemia, and hyponatremia. Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone is markedly elevated. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is most likely responsible?
explanations: Correct. 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the most common cause of CAH; low cortisol and aldosterone with androgen excess cause ambiguous genitalia in a 46,XX infant and a salt-wasting crisis (hyperkalemia, hyponatremia), diagnosed by elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone.

Placental aromatase deficiency causes maternal and fetal virilization from androgen excess, but does not produce the salt-wasting crisis or elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone described here, which are classic for 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
Androgen receptor mutation (CAIS) occurs in 46,XY individuals and produces a female phenotype, not ambiguous genitalia with salt wasting in an XX infant.
5-alpha reductase deficiency occurs in 46,XY individuals (impaired conversion of testosterone to DHT) and does not cause a salt-wasting crisis or ambiguous genitalia in an XX infant.
Swyer syndrome occurs in 46,XY individuals with streak gonads and female external genitalia, unrelated to ambiguous genitalia and salt wasting in an XX infant.
questions.overview: 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, blocking cortisol and aldosterone synthesis while shunting precursors toward androgen production; low cortisol raises ACTH, further driving adrenal androgen excess. In a 46,XX fetus this causes ambiguous genitalia (XX DSD), while low aldosterone produces a life-threatening salt-wasting crisis with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia, diagnosed by an elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone level.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman notes a subtle area of thickening in both breasts without a discrete palpable mass. Mammography is unremarkable. A core needle biopsy of the right breast shows tumor cells infiltrating the stroma in a single-file linear pattern without gland formation. Immunohistochemistry shows loss of E-cadherin expression. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Correct. Invasive lobular carcinoma loses the adhesion protein E-cadherin, causing tumor cells to grow in a discohesive, single-file pattern; it is often multifocal and bilateral.
LCIS is also E-cadherin-negative and discohesive but is non-invasive (does not breach the basement membrane) and is typically an incidental biopsy finding, not an invasive mass.
DCIS is a non-invasive lesion confined by an intact basement membrane and classically produces microcalcifications, not invasive single-file infiltration.
Inflammatory carcinoma presents with peau d'orange skin changes from dermal lymphatic invasion, not with single-file infiltrating cells on biopsy.
Invasive ductal carcinoma typically forms gland-like structures with a desmoplastic stromal reaction rather than single-file cords, and is not characteristically bilateral or E-cadherin-negative.
questions.overview: Invasive lobular carcinoma arises from TDLU epithelium and characteristically loses E-cadherin, causing tumor cells to grow in a single-file pattern rather than forming glands; it is often multifocal and bilateral. This contrasts with invasive ductal carcinoma (most common, ~80%, forms duct-like structures with desmoplastic stroma) and lobular carcinoma in situ (also E-cadherin-negative but non-invasive, an incidental finding and risk factor for future carcinoma in either breast).

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy develops sudden, severe left testicular pain and swelling during soccer practice, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. On examination, the left testicle is high-riding with a transverse lie, and stroking the inner thigh produces no retraction of the scrotum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Emergent surgical exploration with detorsion and orchiopexy
Obtain scrotal ultrasound and schedule elective outpatient urology follow-up
Start oral antibiotics for presumed epididymitis
Reassurance, as this condition typically resolves spontaneously
explanations: NSAIDs and support do not address the mechanical vascular compromise causing torsion and would allow progression to infarction.

Correct. The absent cremasteric reflex and acute painful, high-riding testicle indicate testicular torsion, a surgical emergency requiring urgent detorsion and orchiopexy to prevent infarction and infertility.
Delaying care for elective imaging and outpatient follow-up risks testicular infarction; torsion requires emergent, not elective, intervention.

Epididymitis typically has a more gradual onset, preserved cremasteric reflex, and pain relief with testicular elevation (Prehn sign), unlike this acute presentation with an absent cremasteric reflex.
Torsion does not reliably resolve spontaneously; delay risks hemorrhagic infarction and loss of the testicle.
questions.overview: Testicular torsion results from twisting of the spermatic cord, often due to a bell-clapper deformity, causing venous outflow obstruction while arterial inflow continues, leading to engorgement and hemorrhagic infarction. It presents with acute pain, swelling, and an absent cremasteric reflex, and is a surgical emergency requiring urgent detorsion and orchiopexy (with attention to the contralateral testis) to prevent infertility.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old phenotypic female presents with primary amenorrhea. She has normal breast development but absent axillary and pubic hair. Pelvic examination reveals a blind-ending vaginal pouch with no palpable uterus or cervix. Imaging shows bilateral gonads within the inguinal canals, and karyotype is 46,XY with testosterone in the normal male range. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Kallmann syndrome causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia and absent secondary sexual characteristics (including no breast development), which does not match this presentation.

Correct. In CAIS, an androgen receptor mutation in a 46,XY individual leads to testes that secrete MIF (causing absence of the uterus) and testosterone, but end-organ androgen insensitivity produces a female phenotype with absent pubic/axillary hair, while peripheral aromatization of testosterone causes breast development.

Swyer syndrome involves streak (dysgenetic) gonads rather than descended testes, and testosterone levels are low since functioning Leydig cells are absent, unlike this patient's elevated testosterone and inguinal gonads.
Müllerian agenesis occurs in 46,XX individuals with normal ovaries and normal androgen exposure/pubic hair, and is not associated with inguinal gonads or a 46,XY karyotype.

5-alpha reductase deficiency presents with ambiguous or predominantly female external genitalia that masculinizes at puberty due to elevated testosterone, and internal male structures (vas deferens, seminal vesicles) are present; it does not produce breast development.
questions.overview: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome results from a mutation in the androgen receptor in 46,XY individuals; testes form and secrete Müllerian inhibiting factor (causing absence of the uterus and fallopian tubes) and testosterone, but end-organ unresponsiveness to androgens produces a female external phenotype with absent axillary/pubic hair, while peripheral aromatization of testosterone to estrogen drives breast development at puberty. Patients present with primary amenorrhea, a blind-ending vagina, and abdominal/inguinal undescended testes, with testosterone levels in the normal-to-elevated male range.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old male has not developed facial or axillary hair, has poor muscle development, and reports an inability to smell food. Which of the following best explains this presentation?
options: Primary testicular failure from mumps orchitis
explanations: Correct. Kallmann syndrome is caused by GnRH deficiency due to impaired migration of GnRH neurons, producing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism plus anosmia, predominantly affecting males.
Androgen insensitivity syndrome occurs in phenotypic females (46,XY with female external genitalia), not in males with delayed puberty and anosmia.
Mumps orchitis causes primary (not secondary) hypogonadism and is not linked to anosmia.
Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes primary hypogonadism but is not associated with anosmia.
questions.overview: Kallmann syndrome is caused by a GnRH deficiency due to failure of GnRH neuron migration to the hypothalamus, producing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism combined with anosmia; it predominantly affects males and presents at puberty with failure to develop secondary sexual characteristics such as facial/body hair, muscle mass, and voice deepening.

questions.stem: A newborn is found to be small for gestational age with hepatosplenomegaly and a diffuse petechial 'blueberry muffin' rash. Head CT shows periventricular intracranial calcifications, and the infant fails the newborn hearing screen. Which of the following congenital infections is the most likely cause?
explanations: Congenital toxoplasmosis classically causes hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, and diffuse (not specifically periventricular) intracranial calcifications, and is not the classic infectious cause of congenital deafness.

Correct. CMV is the most common infectious cause of congenital sensorineural deafness and classically causes small size for gestational age, hepatosplenomegaly, blueberry muffin rash, and periventricular intracranial calcifications.

Congenital syphilis presents with rash, rhinorrhea ('snuffles'), and long bone abnormalities early, with later findings like saddle nose and Hutchinson teeth, not this periventricular calcification/deafness pattern.
HSV is transmitted at birth via genital lesions (not transplacentally) and causes vesicular skin lesions with possible CNS/disseminated disease, not this constellation.

Congenital rubella syndrome causes sensorineural deafness, cataracts, PDA, and blueberry muffin baby, but the classic calcification pattern and most common infectious cause of congenital deafness is CMV, not rubella.
questions.overview: Congenital CMV infection is usually asymptomatic at birth but is the most common infectious cause of congenital sensorineural hearing loss, and may also present with small size for gestational age, microcephaly, hepatosplenomegaly, blueberry muffin rash, seizures, and periventricular intracranial calcifications. This contrasts with congenital toxoplasmosis, whose classic triad is hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, and diffuse intracranial calcifications.

questions.stem: Meigs syndrome consists of an ovarian fibroma associated with which two additional findings?
explanations: Hirsutism and amenorrhea are features of androgen-secreting Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors, not fibromas.
Correct. Meigs syndrome is defined by an ovarian fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion, likely due to capillary leak from tumor factors, resolving after tumor removal.
Torsion and hemoperitoneum are not part of the defined Meigs syndrome triad.
Precocious puberty and estrogen excess are features of granulosa cell tumors, not fibromas.
questions.overview: Ovarian fibromas are benign, hormonally-inactive tumors of fibroblasts that typically occur in postmenopausal women and present as a solid, white pelvic mass; ascites occurs in about 40% of cases, and when accompanied by pleural effusion, this constitutes Meigs syndrome, which resolves after surgical removal of the tumor.

questions.stem: A pregnancy category X drug used to treat severe acne is associated with spontaneous abortion, craniofacial abnormalities, congenital heart disease, and hydrocephalus. This drug is:
explanations: Correct. Isotretinoin, a vitamin A derivative used to treat acne, is pregnancy category X, causing spontaneous abortion in about 20% of pregnancies and embryopathy in 20-30% of live births.
Methotrexate causes neural tube defects and craniofacial/limb anomalies via folate inhibition, but it is used as an anti-inflammatory/abortifacient, not for acne.
Lithium is associated with cardiac defects (Ebstein anomaly) and is not used to treat acne.
Warfarin causes fetal hemorrhage, optic atrophy, and bone/cartilage abnormalities, and is not used to treat acne.
questions.overview: Isotretinoin, a vitamin A derivative used to treat severe acne, is a pregnancy category X teratogen requiring mandatory birth control during use; it causes spontaneous abortion in about 20% of exposed pregnancies and 'embryopathy' (abnormal facial features, congenital heart disease, hydrocephalus) in 20-30% of live births. Excess vitamin A itself carries similar first-trimester teratogenic risk at supra-therapeutic doses.

questions.stem: Caudal regression syndrome (sacral agenesis), classically seen in infants of insulin-dependent diabetic mothers and sometimes including sirenomelia, is often associated with which additional finding?
explanations: Cleft lip/palate is not specifically linked to caudal regression syndrome in the notes.
Holoprosencephaly results from Sonic hedgehog pathway mutations affecting forebrain cleavage, not linked to maternal diabetes in the notes.
Correct. Caudal regression syndrome often includes a neural tube defect in addition to incomplete sacral development and possible sirenomelia.
Amniotic band syndrome is an extrinsic disruption from fibrous bands, unrelated to maternal diabetes.
questions.overview: Maternal diabetes is teratogenic through multiple mechanisms, causing macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, congenital heart defects, and caudal regression syndrome (sacral agenesis) — classically seen in infants of insulin-dependent mothers — which may include sirenomelia ('mermaid syndrome') and often a neural tube defect.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl presents with abdominal pain and a palpable pelvic mass. Ultrasound shows a large, solid ovarian mass with areas of necrosis and hemorrhage. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is markedly elevated, and biopsy reveals glomerulus-like structures. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Correct. The yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor secretes alpha-fetoprotein and shows pathognomonic Schiller-Duval bodies (glomeruloid structures), presenting as a large, necrotic, hemorrhagic mass, often in young children.
Granulosa cell tumor secretes estrogen and shows Call-Exner bodies on histology, not AFP or Schiller-Duval bodies.
Dysgerminoma shows undifferentiated germ cells with a 'fried egg' appearance and may secrete LDH or hCG but not AFP, and does not show Schiller-Duval bodies.
Choriocarcinoma secretes hCG rather than AFP and consists of syncytiotrophoblast/cytotrophoblast cells without villi or glomeruloid structures.
Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) is typically an asymptomatic, benign mass containing hair, skin, and sebaceous material, not a necrotic AFP-secreting mass.
questions.overview: The yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor is a malignant germ cell tumor derived from extraembryonic yolk sac cells that secretes alpha-fetoprotein and shows pathognomonic Schiller-Duval bodies (glomeruloid structures) on histology; it presents as a large, hemorrhagic/necrotic mass and can occur in the ovary of young girls or the testis of young boys. AFP serves as a useful tumor marker for diagnosis and monitoring, analogous to hCG for choriocarcinoma and gestational trophoblastic disease.

questions.stem: Which cell type and secreted factor are responsible for regression of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts in a normal male fetus?
options: Sertoli cells secreting Müllerian inhibitory factor
explanations: Leydig cells secrete testosterone, which stimulates (not suppresses) the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts.
hCG is a placental hormone unrelated to Müllerian duct regression.
Granulosa cells are ovarian supporting cells and are not relevant to male duct regression.
Correct. Sertoli cells secrete Müllerian inhibitory factor (MIF), which suppresses development of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts in males.
questions.overview: In male genital development, Sertoli cells secrete Müllerian inhibitory factor (MIF), causing regression of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts, while Leydig cells secrete androgens that stimulate the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts to differentiate into the epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and ejaculatory ducts. In the absence of MIF and androgens, the paramesonephric ducts persist and form the fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper vagina.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation by last menstrual period presents with hyperemesis gravidarum and new hypertension. Her uterus is larger than expected for dates. Serum hCG is markedly elevated (>200,000 mIU/mL). Ultrasound shows a diffuse 'snowstorm' pattern with no fetal parts and bilateral cystic ovarian masses. Genetic analysis of the tissue would most likely reveal which karyotype?
explanations: 47,XXY is the karyotype of Klinefelter syndrome and is unrelated to molar pregnancy.

Correct. A complete mole results from fertilization of an empty ovum by a sperm that duplicates its genome, producing a 46,XX karyotype entirely of paternal origin with no fetal tissue, the most common form of molar pregnancy.
45,X is the karyotype of Turner syndrome and is unrelated to molar pregnancy.

A 69,XXX triploid karyotype is characteristic of a partial mole (fertilization of a normal egg by two sperm), which typically has some fetal tissue present, inconsistent with the complete absence of fetal parts here.
A normal diploid conceptus would produce a fetus and normal villi on ultrasound, not the snowstorm appearance with absent fetal parts described here.
questions.overview: A complete hydatidiform mole results from fertilization of an empty (enucleate) ovum, typically by a single sperm that duplicates its genome, yielding a 46,XX karyotype entirely of paternal origin with no fetal tissue and diffusely swollen chorionic villi ('cluster of grapes,' 'snowstorm' on ultrasound). It presents with markedly elevated hCG, size-greater-than-dates, hyperemesis, theca lutein cysts, and possible hyperthyroidism/preeclampsia, and carries a higher risk of subsequent choriocarcinoma than a partial mole.
